title: The collar
hookLine: a man rages against his vocation until he hears "Child!" and answers "My Lord" (The Collar)
tomorrow: can sweeping a floor be a prayer? Herbert has a line for that.

cards: Some days end with a message typed and deleted: I quit. George Herbert wrote a poem that starts right there. "I struck the board, and cried, No more. I will abroad."
He wants out. His life feels like a cage, his harvest only thorns. And the lines run ragged and loud, one complaint tumbling over the next.

teach.b: Herbert had hoped for a life at court, Walton tells, before he became a country priest, and some readers hear that in The Collar.
Even the title has more than one sound: a priest's collar, a collar that holds you back, and some readers hear choler, an old word for anger. The poem lets the anger run, uneven and wild.
Then: "But as I rav'd and grew more fierce and wild At every word, Methought I heard one calling, Child! And I replied, My Lord."
One word, and the rage is answered, not argued with.
That's the Christian teaching of adoption: God calls people children, not just servants.
Paul writes in Romans: "ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father." Herbert's rage isn't punished.
It's met with a name. And that closes this camp of poets, from Tagore's butterfly and Basho's road to Issa's dew, Li Bai's moon and Herbert's table.

how: Christians call God Father and speak of being adopted as God's children (Romans 8:15). Herbert's The Collar is read as a prayer that lets anger be said before it is answered.

games.q: a friend thinks being furious at God means she's lost her faith. what fits The Collar?
o: Herbert, a priest, raged in a poem, and it ended in 'Child!' and 'My Lord.'
she's right; people of real faith never feel that way.
the poem says anger proves no one is listening.
games.why: Herbert lets the rage run nearly the whole poem. it ends not in punishment but in a name: Child, and his answer, My Lord.

practice: Make two fists, and feel what's tight in you today: a grievance, a no more. Hold it for one breath. Then open your hands, palms up, and leave them resting open while you sit.
Nothing to fix; let one rage settle.
